strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations of existing approaches (token limits, cross-row/column dependency capture, long prompt issues)
Substantial empirical improvements on sub-table selection: 51.2% precision vs. ITR's 16.4% (+34.8pp), with 97.8% recall
Stable performance across varying table sizes (Table 6), a significant advantage over TabSQLify which degrades with size
Thoughtful data generation strategy with balanced target window size distribution to address class imbalance
Comprehensive ablation studies validating design choices: fine-tuning vs. in-context learning, target format (table vs. index), and data balancing
Clear algorithmic presentation with well-specified procedures (Algorithms 1-2) and effective visual illustrations
End-to-end table QA improvement of 1.51% over baseline (88.55% vs. 87.04% with ITR), demonstrating practical utility
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Single-dataset evaluation only (WikiSQL). No evaluation on Spider, HybridQA, SQA, or other standard table QA benchmarks. Standard practice in table QA requires multi-dataset validation
CRITICAL: Window size w=3 is not ablated or justified. This is arguably the most important hyperparameter. Missing sensitivity analysis (w=2,4,5,6) makes results potentially unstable

CRITICAL: Union vs. gold table analysis lacks rigor. Section 3.3 claims union performs 'on par' with gold, but Table 1 shows 91.25% vs. 93.13% (1.88% gap). More importantly, there is an unresolved tension: union achieves only 51.2% precision yet comparable QA performance to gold tables. Why irrelevant rows don't hurt QA deserves theoretical justification

Convergence and iteration analysis incomplete. Algorithm 1 terminates when T^{t-1}=T^t, but paper only shows iter. 1 vs. iter. 2 (Table 2). How many iterations typical? When does iter. 3+ help? Unanalyzed

No computational efficiency measurements despite claiming efficiency advantage. Missing: wall-clock time, memory usage, token counts. Iterative refinement may actually be slower than single-pass despite fewer tokens per iteration
Training data generation is SQL-specific and dataset-dependent. Unclear how balanced sampling (w=3 specific) generalizes to non-SQL tables or different domains
Incomplete baseline comparison. TabSQLify uses ChatGPT API while PieTa uses fine-tuned Llama3-8B (not directly comparable). Details on model selection ('best results for each') are vague
Limited conceptual novelty. Divide-and-conquer, instruction tuning, and iterative refinement are standard techniques; main contribution is their application to table QA
Output format analysis incomplete. Only compared against index format; many alternatives unexplored. Explanation for why cell values help is superficial
Fundamental evaluation metric tension: Precision/recall computed against 'gold' (intersection) tables, but core claim is that union (non-minimal superset) is better. These frameworks are at odds
Missing important ablations and analyses: prompt sensitivity, per-question-type performance, failure cases, which questions benefit most from approach
WikiSQL has relatively small tables (avg 18.6 rows, 6.4 columns). Claims about handling 'large tables' unsubstantiated

strengths: Clear identification of practical problem: language models struggle with long table contexts due to attention window limits
Comprehensive ablation studies validating design choices (fine-tuning vs. in-context learning, target format, data balancing)
Thoughtful data generation with balanced sampling to address class imbalance in target window sizes
Significant improvement in sub-table selection precision (51.2% vs. 16.4% ITR, 13.7% TabSQLify)
Stable performance across varying table sizes (Table 6), indicating practical robustness
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is straightforward divide-and-conquer with set union merging—standard engineering rather than novel methodology
Union-based design lacks principled justification: Claims it's 'easier' than intersection, but no systematic analysis of failure cases or quantification of precision/recall trade-offs
Severely limited experimental scope: Only WikiSQL evaluated (simple select-aggregate-filter operations); no evaluation on Spider, HybridQA, FeTaQA, or other challenging benchmarks
Modest end-to-end improvements (1.51 percentage points: 87.04%→88.55%) with no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Unfair baseline comparisons: TabSQLify uses in-context learning while PieTa uses fine-tuning on 56K examples—fundamentally different paradigms conflated; Dater mentioned but never directly compared

Critical technical detail missing at test time: Training labels 'condition' and 'answer' columns via SQL annotations, but at test time there is no gold SQL—implicit learning strategy never validated or analyzed
Fixed window size (w=3) with no justification or ablation; no analysis of computational cost despite potentially creating ~1,950² windows for large tables
Convergence behavior underspecified: Table 2 shows dramatic precision jump (22.4%→51.2%) between iterations but convergence analysis, typical iteration counts, and runtime comparisons absent
Section 3.3 reads defensive rather than analytical; single-example Figure 3 insufficient to support union design choice; weak image-pixel analogy to tables lacking spatial locality

Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned, hyperparameters underspecified, balanced sampling relegated to appendix; no sensitivity analysis on key design choices (stride, window size, adaptive sizing)

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-articulated limitations of existing approaches (holistic methods, ITR, Dater/TabSQLify)
Sound and practical divide-and-conquer methodology with intuitive iterative window-based processing that handles long-range dependencies
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with strong ablation studies demonstrating design choices (fine-tuning vs in-context learning, target format, data balancing)
Significant improvements in sub-table selection metrics (51.2% precision vs 16.4% for ITR, 97.8% recall)
Consistent improvements across varying table sizes and configurations (Tables 3-4, 6)
Well-justified union-based approach with concrete illustrative examples (Figure 3)
Good reproducibility with publicly available models/datasets and adequate implementation details
Clear presentation with effective figures, algorithms, and well-organized writing
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—core contribution is relatively straightforward combination of sliding windows, LM fine-tuning, and iterative merging without fundamental algorithmic innovation
Evaluation restricted to single dataset (WikiSQL); lacks generalization evidence on other benchmarks (Spider, FeTaQA, SQA) needed to assess broad applicability
Modest final QA task improvements (only 1.5% over baseline) despite larger sub-table selection gains; significant gap between union table (88.55%) and gold table (93.13%) performance
Missing computational cost analysis—iterative approach requires multiple passes but no runtime/memory comparison provided; efficiency unclear for very large tables
Window size choice (w=3) used without justification or ablation studies; appears somewhat arbitrary
No qualitative failure analysis or systematic understanding of when/why the union approach breaks down; limited error case discussion
Convergence properties not formally analyzed; union-based accumulation could retain irrelevant cells once selected; only achieves local convergence criterion
Training data balancing strategy appears ad-hoc and labor-intensive; generalizability to other datasets unclear
Fair comparison concerns: TabSQLify uses ChatGPT/Llama3-70B while PieTa uses Llama3-8B-Instruct; model size differences not adequately emphasized

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing real limitations of existing table QA approaches (holistic methods, code generation, independent row/column selection)
Novel coordinate-based representation that preserves table structure and outperforms index/table representations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two datasets with multiple readers and baselines, including thorough ablation studies
Strong and consistent empirical results with 47.43% precision improvement over ITR while maintaining high recall (99.12%)
Well-presented paper with effective visualizations (Figures 2-4) and reproducible methodology with detailed appendix
Practical approach that achieves consistent improvements across varying table sizes and reader configurations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution (sliding windows + set union merging) is relatively straightforward engineering solution rather than conceptual breakthrough

Insufficient justification for union-based merging strategy: Section 3.4 acknowledges tables lack spatial locality of images, and Table 1 shows union tables achieve comparable but inferior performance to gold tables (92.64% vs 92.65%)
Narrow evaluation scope: only two Wikipedia-derived datasets; questions about generalization to other domains, table structures, and languages
Requires SQL annotations (SQUALL/WikiSQL) for training, significantly limiting applicability to new domains without such annotations; no discussion of few-shot or unsupervised settings
Missing computational cost analysis despite multiple iterative passes: no timing comparisons, iteration count statistics, or total LM call comparisons with baselines
Incomplete ablation studies: window size selection appears empirical (why 4×4 works best unexplained); impact of data augmentation (8-21% of training data) not fully ablated
Limited error analysis: no concrete failure cases, error patterns, or discussion of when union-based approach hurts performance
Theoretical gaps: convergence properties of Algorithm 1 not analyzed; no guarantee that iterative union eventually captures necessary information

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenges of applying LMs to large tables under token constraints
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two benchmarks with multiple baselines and ablation studies
Useful technical contribution with coordinate-based representation that addresses cascading errors in autoregressive table generation
Consistent empirical improvements on most reader/dataset combinations with extensive implementation details for reproducibility
Clear presentation of methodology with intuitive divide-and-conquer framework
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: windowing over tables is not new, union-based merging is simplistic, and LM fine-tuning is straightforward; coordinate representation addresses known issues but is incremental

Weak justification for key design choices: (1) Union strategy creates 60% precision/99% recall tension inadequately explained; (2) Iterative refinement lacks theoretical justification for why repeating the same selector on progressively smaller tables improves results; (3) Fixed 4×4 window size has no principled basis

Mixed and inconsistent empirical results: underperforms TabSQLify on WikiTQ+TaPEx (58.01% vs 58.75%); performance degradation on tables with 400+ cells undermines core motivation; improvements vary significantly across readers

Training data generation requires multiple annotated datasets (SQUALL, WikiSQL) limiting applicability; manual stratification required (A.5) due to class imbalance suggests lack of robustness; data augmentation poorly justified

Precision-recall tradeoff not adequately addressed: high recall/moderate precision of selected subtables contradicts efficiency claims and goal of focused answer generation; unclear whether improved QA comes from better selection or reader robustness to noisy input

Comparison fairness concerns: different training paradigms (fine-tuning vs in-context learning) make baseline comparison unfair; variable GPT-3.5 configurations; inconsistent use of reproduced vs published results
Limited failure analysis: no discussion of failure modes, problematic question types, or why performance degrades on large tables; no error analysis or case studies
Weak multi-resolution framing: analogy to CNNs/vision transformers is misleading given lack of spatial structure in tables; 'multi-resolution' terminology is imprecise for this windowing approach

Limited scope of evaluation: only Wikipedia-based datasets; unknown generalization to other domains; relatively small by modern standards; no evaluation on truly large-scale or messy real-world tables
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests; single-run experiments; some improvements appear small and may not be statistically significant

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple readers and table sizes with consistent improvements; strong subtable selection precision (60.88% vs 13.45% ITR, 75.47% TabSQLify)
Novel coordinate-based subtable representation that elegantly overcomes limitations of index and table representations, with clear empirical validation (+5.26% over alternatives)
Clear problem motivation articulating genuine limitations of prior work (holistic approaches fail on large tables, ITR cannot capture dependencies, in-context learning suffers from long prompts)
Well-designed methodology with careful training data generation, handling of class imbalance, and multiple ablation studies on key design choices
Excellent presentation, clarity, and reproducibility with detailed algorithms, hyperparameter specifications, and comprehensive appendix enabling recreation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: divide-and-conquer with sliding windows is well-established; contribution is primarily application and engineering rather than a fundamentally new algorithm

Evaluation confined to small, well-structured tables (avg 6-6.4 cols, 18.6-25.8 rows; max 21-23 cols, 517-1950 rows); lacks evaluation on other benchmarks (FeTaQA, Spider, TATQA) and truly large real-world tables

Union vs. gold table trade-off incompletely addressed: union tables select rows matching any condition separately versus gold tables requiring all conditions, with unexplained gaps and insufficient analysis of when union suffices

Insufficient justification of design choices: window size w=4 chosen empirically; why w=5 degrades while w=3 performs equally (Table 6) unexplained; stride fixed to 1 without ablation; convergence criteria never explicit

Training data sensitivity acknowledged but not deeply analyzed: Section A.5 reveals random sampling caused 'meaningless single-column target tables,' suggesting approach may be sensitive to data distribution and balancing schemes

Limited scope of comparison: PieTa uses fine-tuning while baselines use in-context learning; exception case (TabSQLify > PieTa with TaPEx on WikiTQ) noted but unexplained; no ablation of augmentation rates (8% vs 21%)

Insufficient error analysis: no case studies of failure modes; Table 3 shows performance varies with column/row counts but lacks explanation; no analysis of complex cross-column reasoning requirements
Evaluation using only exact match metric without partial credit; subtable selection evaluated against gold ground truth while models target union tables, creating metric mismatch; no human evaluation
